name: Umar Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit door casings and patch timber floors at the Quarry Road clinic extension. I'm fifty-eight, trade certified and have enough years on sites to be trusted with an ordinary room, though I am no master joiner. My partner Maja does part-time home care, and our children are grown; the site rate here is low, Maja's hours change, and we have about three weeks of bills saved. There are only a couple of builders close enough for me to reach by bus. I like seeing a patient room finished; I don't like the weeks when the foreman says work may start tomorrow and then it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a small computer change will not fix the missing weeks on our rota. The clinic still needs doors, and I'd ask the union steward to keep pressing for steadier booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am already worried about money before AI enters it. Three weeks of savings is a thin bridge if the clinic pauses, and Maja cannot simply add more care visits whenever I lose a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting casings and check the next four weeks of site dates with the foreman. In the first year I'll take our missing-hours record to the steward and keep applying for any paid local carpentry shifts posted at the depot noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel tense even in this quiet picture. A small software gain does not make a short wage packet easier to stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the last missing week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We used the little savings meant for the boiler service and put that bill back a month. The money went on food and the bus fare to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own rent and children, so I would tell them honestly but not expect a transfer. I want a reliable rota more than a family rescue.

say: I'd tell the crew **rota gaps** matter more than a small app.
I'd ask the steward for **steadier bookings** while clinic doors still need fitting.
think: Our **three-week reserve** is already too thin for a site pause.
Maja's **variable care hours** cannot replace a lost wage packet.
do: Keep fitting **clinic casings** and check four weeks of site dates.
Bring **missing-hours records** to the steward and apply for local paid shifts.
feel: **Tense** about present income even under mild AI change.
S0.quote: I want a reliable rota more than a family rescue.
fieldNote: Umar's anxiety predates AI: a **missed boiler service** shows how one lost week reaches the household.
He seeks **collective rota pressure** and local paid shifts, while refusing to assume adult children can fund him.

steps.text: Keep fitting door casings at Quarry Road
Take missing-hours records to the union steward
Apply for local paid carpentry shifts on the depot board

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may take estimates and ordering, but the firm should tell us when that changes site bookings. I would ask the union branch for the work pipeline in writing before anyone loses a week without notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If fewer office staff slow or change contracts, my low-paid site hours could be cut again. There are few firms close by, and I cannot pay rent and food from three weeks of savings while waiting for a new system to settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the steward to demand the next contract dates and keep taking clinic shifts. If the firm cancels a second week, I'll apply to the two reachable builders and ask Maja to help me list what bills can wait without risking the heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, and a little cross that the people losing hours are often last to hear. I can still make calls, but the local list is short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bills can wait first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop the Saturday café lunch and delay replacing the worn kitchen chairs. I would not skip rent or the heating bill to make a spreadsheet look balanced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the firm's new software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI and would not volunteer for a screen job I cannot do. If the firm gave paid instruction for a required form, I would follow it, but I would keep my focus on paid carpentry.

say: I'd demand **written contract dates** before software changes site bookings.
I'd ask the union to track **lost workweeks**.
think: My **low-paid site hours** could shrink as office work changes.
Few **reachable builders** and three weeks saved leave little room to wait.
do: Ask the **steward** for contract dates and keep clinic shifts.
Apply to **two builders** after another cancelled week.
Stop **Saturday café lunches** and delay chairs if hours fall.
feel: **Anxious and cross** about short notice, with limited local options.
S1.quote: I would not skip rent or the heating bill to make a spreadsheet look balanced.
fieldNote: His **bill choices** protect rent and heat while cutting café spending first.
The small **local job market** makes a second cancelled week a trigger for applications and union questions.

steps.text: Ask the union steward for written contract dates
Apply to two reachable builders after another cancelled week
Stop Saturday café lunches if shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch that full thinking AI in 2028 may change plans and estimates, but site robots around 2031 are the point when our hands-on jobs are at risk. I would ask for notice and a paid path into whatever work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when office work changes and sixty-three when a robot could fit the clinic doors. We cannot live on my partner Maja's care visits alone, and three weeks of savings leaves almost no room if the builder cuts me before retirement is affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll join the branch meeting on robot safety and ask the foreman for the clinic schedule in writing. In 2029 I'd keep taking paid casings work; if shifts are removed, I'll apply to the two local repair crews and ask the branch whether any funded paid placement is actually available, enrolling only if wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened by the speed, but I have a list of people to call. If those repair crews are full, I do not know how we will cover the months between a layoff and whatever work comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a funded placement need to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough to cover rent, heating and the bus while I learn, not a token allowance. I would want that figure in writing before I leave this low wage for an even lower one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider moving for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maja has care clients here and we cannot spend a deposit on the chance of work elsewhere. I would look at a real paid offer first, then talk through the costs with her.

say: I'd separate **2028 office change** from the 2031 site robot risk.
I'd ask the branch for **notice and paid placements**.
think: At **sixty-three**, robot door fitting could remove the income we need.
Our **three-week savings** cannot carry a long search for work.
do: Attend the **branch meeting** and get a written clinic schedule.
Keep **paid casing work** in 2029 while offered.
Apply to **repair crews** if shifts go and enrol only in a paid placement.
feel: **Frightened**, but still able to make calls and judge offers.
S2.quote: We cannot live on my partner Maja's care visits alone, and three weeks of savings leaves almost no room if the builder cuts me before retirement is affordable.
fieldNote: The **2031 robot date** threatens the household's essential wage before a retirement budget exists.
He considers retraining only with **wages in writing** and cannot afford a speculative move away from Maja's care clients.

steps.text: Attend the union meeting on robot safety and notice
Keep taking paid casing work in 2029
Apply to two local repair crews if shifts are cut
Enrol in repair training only if a funded placement covers essential bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years ought to be enough to negotiate a fair warning system for site workers. I would ask the builder and the union to publish the work calendar every month, not just when trouble comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when robots could do the doors. That gives us more paydays, but low wages and skipped weeks mean I cannot assume we will have enough to stop working by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid clinic and repair shifts and ask the steward for monthly calendars starting now. In 2032 I'd still fit doors if offered; if a month goes unbooked, I'd apply to both local firms and ask the community advice office what support we actually qualify for while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed by the technology, yet the pay packet is still tight. A longer warning only helps if the builder gives us actual shifts in those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the advice office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know what help exists for a worker with missed weeks, and I don't want to assume a benefit will arrive. I'd ask for the benefit rules before counting on any help for weeks without work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you save over five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to leave a little after full weeks, but many months there is nothing left. The immediate job is keeping rent current while we build any cushion we can.

say: I'd seek **monthly work calendars** through the union.
I'd say five years helps only with **actual paid shifts**.
think: At **sixty-six**, robots might meet an unaffordable retirement.
Low pay and **skipped weeks** can erase the value of extra warning.
do: Keep **paid clinic work** and request monthly calendars.
Apply locally and ask the **advice office** about support after an empty month.
feel: Less **rushed** by AI, still squeezed by current wages.
S3.quote: I'd ask for the benefit rules before counting on any help for weeks without work.
fieldNote: Umar treats **public support** as something to verify, not a guaranteed replacement for wages.
Extra years do not erase his **current low pay**, and the plan still centers on paid site work.

steps.text: Ask the union steward for monthly work calendars
Keep taking paid door-fitting work in 2032
Apply to two local firms after an unbooked month
Ask the community advice office about actual eligibility if work stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to train younger workers and bargain over safety before robots come. I would also tell the crew that a distant machine does not pay this week's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when site robots follow. I may still need paid repairs then, because low wages and our tiny savings give me no firm date when I can retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the clinic work and any paid local repair shifts, and ask the union branch to keep pushing for regular booking. In 2037 I'd still fit or repair doors if my hands allow; Maja and I would compare bills with actual income before I stop applying for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about robots being far away, but I am anxious about the next blank week. A ten-year lead does not fill the gap in our account today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help you retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They might help in an emergency, but they already pay for their own families. I would not call that a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could improve this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A reliable four-day week would make more difference than a lecture about tomorrow's robots. Then Maja and I could begin rebuilding the boiler money.

say: I'd use ten years for **training and safety bargaining**.
I'd remind the crew a distant robot cannot pay **this week's wages**.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still need paid door repairs.
At **seventy-one**, retirement remains uncertain with low wages and thin savings.
do: Keep **clinic and repair shifts** while work is available.
Ask the **union branch** for regular booking.
Fit **paid doors in 2037** if needed and check household bills.
feel: **Anxious about current gaps**, though distant robots bring little immediate fear.
S4.quote: A ten-year lead does not fill the gap in our account today.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** changes little about the immediate wage gap and depleted boiler savings.
He continues **paid work** if necessary at sixty-eight and does not treat adult children's help as retirement income.

steps.text: Keep taking paid clinic and repair shifts while fit
Ask the union branch for regular site bookings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because robots could take my door work around 2031 while we still have almost nothing saved. Written notice, paid repair placements and a reliable rota would help us keep rent paid while we search.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what a cancelled day costs on the bus. Sometimes I've already bought the bus fare before the site cancellation call comes, and that money doesn't come back.

headlineQuote: Sometimes I've already bought the bus fare before the site cancellation call comes, and that money doesn't come back.
portrait: Umar is a **fifty-eight-year-old certified** carpenter with mid-level experience on clinic sites.
His low wage, Maja's variable care hours and **three weeks saved** make rota gaps urgent now.
He has **never used AI** and seeks written schedules, union action and paid local work.
He cannot assume **retirement** or adult children's financial help even on the slow timeline.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could remove his door-fitting wage by 2031 with almost no cash reserve.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, paid repair placements and steadier site bookings.
